newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia seen unlikely to enter world grain market.
newsitem.headline: Russia seen unlikely to enter world grain market.

text.p: Russia is unlikely to raid world grain bins any time soon, as livestock numbers hit record low levels and former Soviet republics work out ways to feed themselves, traders and analysts said on Wednesday.
Russia now produces enough grains to meet most of its needs, human and animal, and demand is not expected to rise much in the short to medium term.

"Demand for wheat is relatively stable and I expect this to continue. I think production volumes this year will be enough to meet demand," said Arkady Zlochevsky, chief executive of the private OGO grains firm.
Another senior Moscow-based grain trader said there was no reason to predict big Russian imports in the forseeable future.
"Russia's human grain needs are about 20 million tonnes and Russia has always had enough to meet this," he said.
"It imported so much in the past for feed grains and milling wheat purposes. But that was when Moscow was feeding the Soviet Union, including many Central Asian republics," he added.
Moscow set world grain markets alight in the 1970s, importing as much as 25 million tonnes annually to feed the 15 Soviet republics' human and animal populations.

Russia's Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun has said 1997 imports would be around the same as in 1996, officially put at 5.1 million tonnes. The trader agreed, adding most of these would probably be consumed in Russia's Far East.
"It is very difficult to predict any major imports into Russia this year, except for the Far East," he said.
It is often more efficient to import grain into the Far East than transport it from Russia's own producing regions.
Traders and analysts said unpredictability of grain harvests meant long-term projections were difficult. But animal, as well as human, needs were not expected to increase quickly.

"The question is whether we will start to develop the poultry and cattle industries. Then Russia would have to move to produce more feed grains. Today there is no such movement," the senior trader said.
Official statistics show a collapse in cattle and poultry numbers in the last few years, demonstrating Russian farmers' inability to compete with cheaper and better meat imports.

"There was not the incentive to raise animals if there were going to be problems selling them and competing (with imports) on a price and quality level," said Thomas Wiley, grains specialist at the European Commission delegation in Moscow.
His opinions were not necessarily those of the Commission.
Cattle numbers in Russia last year were 39.7 million, down eight percent from 1995 and the lowest on State Statistics Committee records since 1961. Pig numbers were at their lowest since 1964.

The poultry business fared little better. Numbers slumped 14 percent in 1996 to 423 million. The committee did not give annual data, but the 1996 total was comparable with figures from the early 1970s.
"Any increase in the number of animals in Russia will take time and much will depend on political lobbying," said one Western grain analyst.
This year Moscow may well rely more heavily on Ukraine and Kazakhstan for import needs, with production in both expected to be up on last year's drought-hit disaster.

Russia's own grain harvest is forecast steady with official targets pegged at at least 70 million tonnes net against 69.3 million in 1996 -- itself a recovery from 1995 but still one of the smallest crops in three decades.

Analysts' forecasts for the 1997 wheat crop varied between 34 and 38 million tonnes against 34.9 million in 1996. Farmers appeared to be reacting to market conditions this season and targeting higher food wheat output and less feed grains.

"Farmers may be planting more area to food wheat this year, partly because Russian demand for feed grains is falling," said Vladimir Totsky, deputy director of Russia's Grain Union, a private grouping of traders and producers.

This year's wheat area was up five percent over the year-ago level by June 2 while most other crops including sugar were down sharply. One analyst said roughly 17 million tonnes of the wheat crop would go into food production, nearly meeting needs of around 20 million.
